1:
The date is given without an era, and the voices supply one. Gill reckons from the deportation the prophet dates by, and notes that he says our captivity because he shared it. Wesley and Ellicott both make the tenth of the first month the day the paschal lamb was set aside, and Ellicott draws the inference: the month of the passover was the year's beginning, so the day preparations began suits a vision of the church to come. He rejects a jubilee year: there is no evidence for it, the jubilee opened at the autumn fast, and nothing shows years were counted from jubilees so early. Henry keeps to the interval: fourteen years after the city fell, the clearest prospect of deliverance arrives at the midnight of the captivity.

Two of them frame the vision before any measuring begins. Keil and Delitzsch describe the last nine chapters as a single vision of the new temple, the new ordering of worship and the new division of the land, rounded off in itself and distinct in form from what precedes, yet bound to it as the half of the book in which the promise of salvation is completed. Clarke argues from the exiles' need: with the temple in ruins and no model thought to survive, the minuteness of the description may have been meant to guide the builders of the second, poorer though like in plan. He adds the older Jewish rule, that whatever was august in prophecy and unfulfilled near its own time was referred to the days of the Messiah.

Nobody takes the journey as bodily. Wesley says the phrase proves the transport was not corporeal, and Ellicott makes those words a standing signal that what follows is ideal description, a symbolic representation rather than a report of anything with literal existence. The mountain then divides them. Clarke identifies it with the hill where the old temple stood; Ellicott denies the description can fit that hill, ringed as it is by higher ground, and takes the height for a mark of the site's spiritual importance. He corrects a preposition so that the structure stands upon the mountain rather than beside it, and explains the southward bearing: a traveller from Chaldea enters the country at the north.

Henry says what the thing seen is. Set on the height as Moses was above the plains, the prophet looks over a land promised a second time and not yet possessed, and sees the frame of a city that turns out to be a temple as large as a city. The last vision of Scripture, he observes, shows a city with no temple in it, and this a city that is nothing but temple — much the same thing, a city for men to live in and a temple for God to live in.

The figure with the instruments is identified variously. Clarke describes polished brass throwing back the light, guesses at a glory about the head, and leaves the choice open between an angel and Christ himself. Henry closes it, making him not a created angel but the one found in fashion as a man so that he might both show the gospel temple and build it; Wesley agrees, identifying him with the figure of the opening vision, whose name is the Branch. Ellicott stays with the tools, giving the flaxen line the long measures and the rod the short.

The charge is read for its manner as much as its content. Gill lingers on the title son of man, which reminds the prophet of his smallness and teaches the humility without which nothing is learned, while the familiarity of the address removes the terror of such an appearance. Clarke keeps the practical end in view: all is to be told to the house of Israel so they may know how to build when the captivity is over.
5:
Everything downstream depends on the rod, and no two agree on its length. Henry makes the reed six cubits of the sanctuary, that cubit being a handbreadth longer than the common, twenty-two inches against eighteen; he reports the rival view, that the reed was six common cubits with one handbreadth added, and prefers his own. Ellicott insists on the same distribution, each of the six cubits carrying its own handbreadth, and explains the addition: the cubit in ordinary use after the return differed from the older standard, so the prophet marks which he means. He declines to fix the figure, estimates running from eighteen inches to twenty-four, and settles on twenty, giving a rod of about ten feet. Clarke reaches ten feet six by a cubit of twenty and a half inches plus a palm; Wesley keeps the common eighteen.

The wall is measured before any gate. Gill notes it is the first thing shown after the architect, and reads it by the purpose stated later in the chapter, to divide the sanctuary from the profane place, which he glosses as the church from the world. Henry gives it three yards each way and draws both consequences, separation and protection, adding that if such a thickness will not secure the place God will be a wall of fire round it. Clarke infers from its being as broad as high that it was a parapet carried all round; Ellicott says the equality is there for symmetry, and notes that the wall's length is withheld until near the end of the chapter. Wesley makes it the outermost wall of the whole hill.

The east gate comes first, and Henry explains why: entry was at the lower end because the holiest place stood at the west, against the heathen habit of worshipping toward the sunrise. He notices too what is not measured, the outer court of the Gentiles, left out, on a suggestion he reports, because the confluence of Gentiles in gospel times would leave its worshippers past numbering. The approach is by stairs. Clarke observes that a building on rising ground needs steps outside each door, and that the chapter has them between court and court as well; Wesley points out that the threshold could not be measured until the surveyor had climbed, the count coming out at ten, eight or seven according to where one supposes him standing.

The little chambers along the gateway divide the readings. Keil and Delitzsch keep to the plan, a rod square apiece with five cubits between and three to each side. Wesley makes them lodgings for priests and Levites during their courses, takes the gaps as either filled with posts or left void, and adds rails set a cubit in front for benches. Gill refuses both obvious spiritual readings, the heart of the believer and the mansions of heaven, and makes them the particular congregations planted in every quarter, called chambers for their secrecy, since the hidden ones are there.

The last details are read the same two ways. Wesley works out that each chamber had a door east and west, set so exactly that with all open one could see through to the house; on the sixty-cubit posts he takes the figure for height and supposes two storeys above the arch. Gill reports the older opinion that those posts stood between the outer wall and the building for ornament, and prefers the columns carrying the arch of the gate, sixty cubits being their height. The narrow windows he explains mechanically and then allegorically: the walls were splayed inside and out so the light admitted should spread further, and since the chambers are the churches, the windows are the word and ordinances by which light gets into them. Wesley says only that they narrowed inward, with more set under the arches.
17:
The outer court is entered, and who used it is answered differently. Ellicott is careful: the plan has two courts and assigns neither to any class of worshipper, though from size and arrangement the inner may be assumed for the priests and the outer for the people. Gill assigns it anyway, matching the old court where good and bad worshipped together, and takes it for the visible church with its wheat and tares.

Chambers and paving run round it, and the arithmetic is disputed. Keil and Delitzsch describe cells and a mosaic floor on both sides of the gate-buildings, of a width matching their length, so the paving did not cover the whole area. Ellicott points out that neither size nor position is given for the thirty chambers, and reasons from the symmetry to ten on each of the three free sides; such rooms, for priests and for storing tithes, are mentioned in both earlier houses. Wesley distributes them otherwise, fifteen each side of the gate, making them store-houses as well as lodgings.

Why the paving is called lower gets two answers, and Gill offers both: it may lie below the paving of the inner court, reached by steps, or its middle may have risen in a slight convex so that water carried the dirt to the sides. Ellicott takes the first, contrasting an inner pavement on a higher level; Wesley takes the second, adding that it served for state as well as cleanliness. Gill then makes the two levels the believer's walk by faith and his walk in the ordinances.

The hundred cubits between the gates are measured three times, and Ellicott finds an ambiguity. The starting point is stated exactly, the innermost end of the outer gate-building; the finishing point is not, so it is open whether the measure ran to the wall of the inner court or only to the outer end of its gate — a doubt he resolves from the later verses, which say from gate to gate. Wesley concludes the court was square, and notes that a diversity of courts may recall the diversity of gifts in the church.

The remaining gates go by their likeness to the first. Keil and Delitzsch remark that the northern and southern buildings are described briefly, the principal parts only, with a note that they matched the east; Clarke says the same measures were used throughout, and corrects a term: what is called an arch should be a porch, the arch being unknown then. Gill turns the repetition into doctrine, that the churches of the latter day will be built on one pattern. Henry presses the uniformity further, that the inner gates matched the outer down to the engraving on the posts, so the work of grace is the same in the grown Christian as in the beginner; and he observes that neither court has a gate on the west, though western porters imply the first house had one and a historian says the second had none.

Inside the inner court one verse defeats both critics, who attack it differently. Ellicott first notes that these gates are the earlier ones reversed, with the porches facing each other, and that they have one step more than the outer, so the two flights make the fifteen which in the later house led from court to court. Then comes the verse giving the arches as twenty-five cubits by five. Clarke treats it as damaged: the breadth ought to read twenty-five, as the parallel verses show, and the word for twenty has dropped out; the whole verse, he adds, is missing from several manuscripts, one of them his own, where a later hand supplied it in the margin. Ellicott suspects the verse itself: the term should mean wall projections, the dimensions fit nothing, the statement is unparalleled among the gates, and the Greek omits it.
38:
The sacrificial fittings are described at the north gate, and Ellicott explains why there. Under the law every offering was killed at the north side of the altar and each offerer killed his own; here the Levites do it, so the work is placed where the offerer and the people can watch, inside the outer court but at that gate. Keil and Delitzsch set out the arrangement as the text gives it: a cell with its door where the burnt offering was washed, two tables on each side within the porch and two more at each shoulder outside, eight in all, with four of hewn stone by the steps to carry the instruments.

The count is not agreed. Ellicott separates the eight tables of one verse from the four and four of another and arrives at twelve, and would read by the porch rather than in it, the porch being too small for two tables a side and a thoroughfare no place to kill an animal. Gill sets the first four in the gaps between the little chambers, two to a side, and treats the later verses as the same tables named again so their position and use may be observed more carefully.

Henry takes the tables for the point of the whole passage. No altar is described until a much later chapter, and he thinks the delay deliberate, since the one altar of the law was to give way to a multitude of tables, and since in this house no altar appears until the glory has taken possession, Christ being himself the altar that sanctifies the gift. Nothing of the kind, he observes, is recorded in the tabernacle or the first temple; the provision here intimates how many spiritual sacrifices would be brought and how many hands employed.

The hooks are a doubtful word. Ellicott notes that it occurs only once elsewhere, where it is rendered pots, and that whatever it means stands within the porch and so cannot belong to the tables outside; he accepts the traditional sense, hooks on which the flesh was hung once it had been prepared. Gill takes them for fittings on the gate posts near the washing room, and describes the later slaughter house: stone pillars carrying cedar boards, three rows of iron hooks a handbreadth out, a lamb hung on the lowest row, a ram on the middle, a bullock on the highest. Wesley has them fastened to walls near the tables, for hanging the carcass while it was further prepared.

The chambers that follow are for singers and keepers. Gill makes the singers the believers who sing with the spirit and the understanding, and thinks their place in the inner court fits them as inward-court worshippers; Wesley identifies the keepers as those in charge of the house during their courses, and the others as keeping the fire alight on the altar. Clarke names the court that is measured here the priests' court.

The porch of the house closes the chapter, and two things are said about it. Gill reads it as a covering from wind and storm and from the heat of the sun, so an emblem of the hiding place from tempest and from a fiery law, and adds that it was thought a place where the priests prayed before going in. Clarke observes that the gate was evidently a folding door, and gives a historian's dimensions for the vestibule at twenty cubits by ten; Keil and Delitzsch record it at twenty by eleven, with a pillar at either post and steps up to it. Gill ends with editorial common sense: these last two verses belong with what follows, and a new chapter ought properly to have begun here.
